strengths: Novel problem formulation: First to explicitly address high-resolution image editing with diffusion models, clearly distinguishing it from standard generation and super-resolution
Sound and well-motivated technical approach: Transfer function learning to inject fine-grained details through diffusion trajectories is intuitive and technically correct
Comprehensive methodology: Systematically addresses practical challenges including detail injection, patch consistency, and content preservation through novel synchronization mechanisms
Strong experimental results: Consistently outperforms diffusion-based SR baselines across multiple metrics (HaarPSI, M-MSE, M-SSIM, M-PSNR) with properly masked variants
Excellent reproducibility: Provides pseudocode (Algorithm 1), detailed mathematical formulations, implementation details using PyTorch, and references to official codebases
Clear presentation with effective visualizations: Figures 1-5 effectively communicate the task and method; qualitative results clearly demonstrate capability
weaknesses: Severely limited evaluation scope: Tested exclusively on AI-generated synthetic images with no evaluation on real photographs or natural images, fundamentally limiting claims about real-world applicability

Missing computational cost analysis: No discussion of memory, runtime, or computational complexity; no inference time comparison with baselines despite patch-wise optimization potentially being expensive

Incomplete baseline comparisons: Only compares against diffusion-based SR methods (DiT-SR, DiT4SR, PISA-SR, TSD-SR); missing comparisons with recent instruction-based editing methods, FLUX, and the naive baseline (edit then super-resolve)

Weak perceptual and semantic evaluation: No user studies to validate quality claims; metrics inadequate for measuring semantic correctness of edits; unclear how well fine-grained details are actually preserved on real content
Limited hyperparameter analysis: Only hyperparameter τ is ablated; synchronization strategy components (blended Tweedie weights, resampling) lack justification and sensitivity analysis
Acknowledged limitations unaddressed: Section G admits suboptimal results due to pretrained model constraints and artifacts from low-resolution translation methods but proposes no solutions

Insufficient theoretical justification: Why transfer functions effectively capture fine-grained details remains unclear; no visualization of learned transfers; no explanation for advantage over direct high-resolution training
Dataset limitations: Only 400 image-text pairs; limited to specific edit types; edits generated via ChatGPT without diversity analysis or quality control metrics
Patch synchronization complexity unjustified: Complex mechanism with blended Tweedie updates and resampling lacks ablation against simpler alternatives
Missing failure case analysis: No visual demonstration of failure modes or artifacts despite acknowledged limitations; only shows successful results

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem: addresses high-resolution image editing with fine-grained control in an intuitive and useful way
Sound technical approach: proper application of diffusion models, null-text inversion, and learnable transfer functions with mathematically rigorous formulation

Comprehensive experimental validation: includes multiple resolution scenarios, diverse metrics (MSE, SSIM, PSNR, LPIPS, HaarPSI), ablation studies demonstrating component importance, and qualitative results showing detail preservation
Thorough ablation studies: Tables 2-3 and Figures 5, 9 clearly demonstrate the contribution of synchronization strategy and design choices
Good generalization: demonstrated applicability across multiple backbone architectures (Stable Diffusion, FLUX) suggesting broader utility
Clear presentation: well-written with effective figures (especially Figures 2-3) explaining the method pipeline and synchronization strategy
Implementation transparency: provides algorithm pseudocode, detailed hyperparameter specifications, and supplementary material with additional details
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (diffusion models, null-text inversion, feature transfer) without fundamental algorithmic innovations; transfer function is simple 1×1 convolution

High computational cost: requires 20.29 GB GPU memory with runtime of 0.74-88.06 sec for 1K and 8.40-36.00 sec for 2K; no direct runtime comparisons with baselines provided; significantly limits practical deployment
Dated baseline comparisons: primary baselines (DIT-SR, DIT4SR) from 2022; recent diffusion-based SR methods and LoRA-based editing approaches mentioned in related work but not empirically compared

Limited evaluation scope: only 100 AI-generated source images; almost exclusively artistic/fantasy imagery with minimal diversity; no evaluation on natural photographs or real-world images; no user studies for perceptual quality validation

Fundamental methodological dependency: method inherits limitations from low-resolution editing; if low-res result is poor, high-res output is constrained; limited discussion of failure modes when low-res editing fails semantically

Insufficient design justification: limited explanation for why 1×1 convolution suffices for transfer function; synchronization weight scheme (Eq. 12) appears empirically derived rather than principled; hyperparameter exploration limited

Artifact persistence: Figure 9 clearly shows boundary artifacts despite synchronization; blended Tweedie helps but doesn't fully eliminate visible seams; some magnified regions show remaining blending artifacts

Reproducibility gaps: no code provided in submission; hyperparameter selection process vague; feature modification term architecture incompletely specified; transfer function training procedure lacks detail

Limited failure case analysis: Section H acknowledges limitations but provides few concrete failure examples; systematic failure mode taxonomy absent; no analysis of when patch-wise editing conflicts with semantic coherence
